newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine October inflation seen at 5.28 pct-poll.
newsitem.headline: Philippine October inflation seen at 5.28 pct-poll.

text.p: Philippine inflation is expected to spike up to a year-on-year 5.28 percent in October after reaching a year-low of 4.4 percent in September, largely due to a recent increase in domestic oil prices, according to a Reuter poll of six institutions.
Inflation in October 1995 was 11.0 percent due to a severe rice shortage. The government is scheduled to announced the figure for this October on November 5.

Ces Tanchoco, a Bank of the Philippine Islands economist, said the rate would rise this October even though fuel and light makes up only three to four percent of the consumer price index as traders would take advantage of fuel prices to raise prices.
"Speculative activities would impact a lot more. The middle market, or the traders, would jack up prices," Tanchoco said.

The impact of the fuel price increases would be felt only towards the latter part of the year because current inventories of fuel were still based on old prices, said Emma Pante, an economist at Far East Bank and Trust Co.

In mid-October, the government's Energy Regulatory Board raised prices of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and diesel oil. These will affect the larger portion of the population since LPG is used for cooking, while diesel is used heavily in the transport sector.
The price of diesel oil rose 50 centavos to 7.57 pesos per litre, while LPG rose 11.13 centavos to 5.95 pesos per litre.

At an average of 30.72 centavos per litre, the rise was the largest since the government adopted a monthly automatic oil pricing mechanism three months ago to pave the way for the full deregulation of the energy sector by March 1997.
In August, prices declined by an average of 9.27 centavos per litre but rose in September by an average of 6.95 centavos.

"The real pressure on inflation is the cost-push... on the supply side. At this point, there is no pressure from the fiscal and monetary side," said Rolando Valenzuela, senior vice president of Philippine TA Securities.

He said the government enjoys a budget surplus and money supply remains below the ceiling set in an agreement with the International Monetary Fund, which should keep interest rates at comfortable levels.
But pressure could come from employees as they push for higher wages because of the increase in oil prices, he said.

For the rest of the year, increased spending for the Christmas season would keep inflation in a 5.0 to 6.0 percent range, still at single-digit levels compared to the double-digit figures experienced from September last year up to May, analysts said.
For all of 1996, the government has revised upwards its average inflation target to 8.7 from 8.5 percent.
Following are the forecasts for October:
Bank of the Philippine Islands 5.4
Far East Bank 5.0
Peregrine Securities 5.0 to 6.0
Philippine TA Securities 5.0 to 5.2
Union Bank 5.3 to 5.5
University of Asia and the Pacific 5.0 to 5.5
